title: Salman Khan Dragged a Movie to Court Over a Blue Bracelet. On June 19, the Delhi High Court Decides Who Owns a Superstar's Face.
excerpt: A film called Kala Hiran tried to dramatize the 1998 blackbuck case. Its lead actor walked out, a veteran co-star says he was misled, and now Salman Khan wants the whole thing buried — testing how far personality rights stretch in India.
body:
It came down to a bracelet. A blue one. The kind **Salman Khan** has worn for decades, the kind fans can sketch from memory, the kind that turns up on a poster and tells you exactly whose story you're about to watch — even when no name is spoken.

That poster dropped on May 29. It showed a character with an uncanny resemblance to Khan, wearing that unmistakable accessory, promoting a film titled **Kala Hiran: The Battle for Legacy** — a thinly fictionalized retelling of the 1998 blackbuck poaching case that has shadowed the actor for over a quarter-century. By June 13, Salman Khan's lawyers were standing before the Delhi High Court asking a judge to make the whole project disappear. On June 19, she'll decide.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=y7invfaKSIw</youtube>


## The Bracelet Argument

Representing Khan, senior advocate **Dayan Krishnan** and advocate Nizam Pasha argued that the film doesn't just reference the actor — it impersonates him. The teaser features a character named Ayaan Khan, played by Kashif Iqbal Khan, whose "appearance, mannerisms, clothing style, and accessories closely resemble those of the superstar." The plea language is pointed:

> "The character depicted has an uncanny resemblance to the plaintiff and is clearly seen wearing a bracelet, which is immediately and promptly identifiable with the plaintiff and no one else."

The legal hook is sharper than mere likeness. Khan's team says the film violates a Delhi High Court order from December 11, 2025, that already granted protection to his personality rights — the bundle of legal protections, increasingly recognized in Indian courts, that lets a public figure control the commercial use of their name, image, voice, and identifiable attributes. If that order means anything, his lawyers argue, it means a film can't build a character out of his face and his bracelet and his most notorious legal chapter, and then sell tickets to it.

There's a second layer: Khan was acquitted under the Arms Act in the broader saga, and his counsel contends the film risks misleading the public about what actually happened in a matter that remains, in parts, *sub judice*. Justice **Neena Bansal Krishna**, sitting on a vacation bench, issued notices to producer **Amit Jani**, Jani FireFox Films, director Bharat Shrinate, casting director Akshay Pandey, and others. The next hearing: June 19.

## The Cast Is Running for the Exits

What makes this more than a routine injunction fight is that the film appears to be collapsing from the inside. Lead actor **Sonu Mishra** publicly exited, and his account is damning. He says he shot for two days, then asked to see the script and contract — and didn't like what he found.

> "It was revealed that I had to speak negatively against the star in the media. So, all these things were against my ethics." — Sonu Mishra

He describes a project built around a "one-sided narrative" against a superstar, with obligations baked into the contract he refused to sign. Veteran actor **Govind Namdev** distanced himself too, saying he believed he was only shooting a courtroom portion and was uncomfortable with what later came to light. "I cannot consider any Bishnoi gang as my ideal," he said, referencing the gang-war undertones the film allegedly leans into — a charged subject given the real threats Khan has faced in recent years.

The makers, for their part, have called the project a work of fiction. But the optics are difficult: a trailer launched on June 13, reportedly ahead of an earlier-planned June 20 unveiling, even as the legal cloud thickened. A film loudly insisting it isn't about Salman Khan, while its own departing actors say otherwise, is not a comfortable position to argue from.

## Why the Diaspora Should Watch June 19

This isn't just gossip-page fodder. India's courts have spent the last few years building out personality-rights doctrine case by case — Amitabh Bachchan, Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff, and others have all won protections for their names, faces, and signature traits. A ruling that stops **Kala Hiran** would harden that protection considerably; one that lets it proceed would carve out room for "fictionalized" portrayals of real, recognizable people drawn from real, ongoing cases.

For a global film industry where deepfakes, AI likenesses, and unauthorized biopics are no longer hypothetical, where the line falls matters far beyond Mumbai. The question in front of Justice Krishna sounds almost philosophical, but the stakes are concrete: how much of a superstar's identity belongs to the superstar — and how much is fair game for anyone with a lookalike, a blue bracelet, and a release date? We find out June 19.
